solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Mark, Susan, Carol and Richard, all leaders (4)

indicatorNotes.all leaders: the leader of each word is the letter at its front, so every name gives up its first letter

annotation.surface: A roll call of four friends, all of them in charge of something.
annotation.walkthrough: Mark looks like the first name on the list, so a solver takes its M too; it is the definition, and even 'and' contributes a leader.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the mark an old wound leaves on the skin.

entries.clue: Preserve courage (6)

blocks.note: keep fruit by sealing it in glass jars

annotation.surface: Keep your nerve.
annotation.walkthrough: The courage sense is British slang, as in 'he lost his bottle'.
annotation.definitionFit: One sense is sealing food in jars to keep it; the other is British slang for nerve.

entries.clue: Person nudging past landing area – revealing game? (5,5)

indicatorNotes.past: to go past something is to come after it, so the nudger follows the landing area

annotation.surface: Someone elbowing their way past an aircraft landing zone.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: the game is revealing because losers shed clothes.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheeky description: losing hands cost items of clothing, so the game reveals the players.

entries.clue: Found outside posh royal house (6)

indicatorNotes.outside: the word for 'found' is placed outside, wrapped round, the letter for 'posh'

blocks.note: to found a company is to start it

annotation.surface: A grand dynasty discovered outside something smart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the past of find; here it is the verb meaning establish.
annotation.definitionFit: A royal house by name: the dynasty that ruled Scotland and later England in the 1600s.

entries.clue: Go Nine, Ten, Queen, King in fish? (8)

blocks.note: to go off quickly, as in leaving town
the card missing from this run

annotation.surface: A card-game instruction: play nine, ten, queen and king.
annotation.walkthrough: The run of cards goes nine, ten, queen, king with the jack left out, so the sequence itself acts out leaving that card behind.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is a kind of tuna.

entries.clue: Indian sovereign has not shut up! (4)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' means read the word from bottom to top

annotation.surface: An outraged cry that a ruler just will not stop talking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' reads as an order to be quiet; the phrase splits into 'not shut' and the reversal signal 'up'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the title of an Indian king or prince.

entries.clue: Notice in criminal something toxic (8)

indicatorNotes.criminal: something criminal is bent or wrong, so the letters are put in a crooked order

annotation.surface: A warning notice spotted among a criminal's poisonous goods.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a verb in the surface; it is just letters, with 'in' taken along as well.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the drug in tobacco is a poison in larger doses.

entries.clue: Old military leader going on foot? (10)

blocks.note: the duke who won at Waterloo
a rubber boot, named after that duke

annotation.surface: A retired general who now travels by walking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going on foot' sounds like walking; it means something that goes on your foot, the boot named after the Duke.
annotation.definitionFit: One sense is the victor of Waterloo; the other is the boot, which goes on a foot.

entries.clue: Influence strike (5)

annotation.walkthrough: Both words can be nouns or verbs; the answer works as a noun for the first and a verb for the second.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: power to sway people, and a heavy blow.

entries.clue: On yer bike – or walk (4,1,4)

blocks.note: rude British way of saying go away

annotation.surface: Someone told to get lost, whether cycling or on foot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On yer bike' is British slang for go away, so both halves are brush-offs dressed up as ways of travelling.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: both phrases dismiss someone, and the second also literally means a long walk.

entries.clue: Bit of a looker necks second wine (7)

indicatorNotes.necks: to neck a drink is to swallow it, so the eye part takes the letter inside

blocks.note: part of an eye, which looks

annotation.surface: An attractive person downing another glass of wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Looker' suggests a pretty person; here it is an eye. 'Necks' is British slang for drinks quickly.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Greek white wine flavoured with pine resin.

entries.clue: Bird in flap, we gathered, around duck (7)

indicatorNotes.gathered: gathered things are collected up in a new arrangement, so the letters regroup
indicatorNotes.around: the regrouped letters are placed around the letter for duck

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

annotation.surface: A panicking group huddled round a duck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flap' reads as a panic; it is simply fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the peacock and peahen together.

entries.clue: Discount, price finally secured by gentleman (5)

annotation.definitionNote: Discount here is the adjective, as in a discount store.

indicatorNotes.finally: finally means at the end, so take the last letter
indicatorNotes.secured by: something secured by a holder is held inside it

annotation.surface: A reduced price guaranteed by a gentleman's word.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discount' looks like a noun, a price cut; it works as the adjective in 'discount goods'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: discount goods are low-priced.

entries.clue: Clown’s prop pictured as funny (7,3)

indicatorNotes.funny: funny can mean odd, so the letters come out in an odd order

annotation.surface: A clown's equipment shown to be comic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Funny' sits naturally beside a clown, which hides its job as the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: clowns throw these into each other's faces.

entries.clue: Serious actor was furious, one caught by whip (9)

indicatorNotes.caught by: something caught by another is held inside it, so the whip surrounds the rest

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them

annotation.surface: A dramatic actor lost his temper after being lashed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tan' for beat comes from tanning leather, and survives in 'tan someone's hide'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: an actor who plays tragic, serious roles.

entries.clue: His anger out of control about graduate lecturing (10)

indicatorNotes.out of control: letters out of control run wild into a new order
indicatorNotes.about: the new arrangement sits about, around, the letters for graduate

annotation.surface: A man loses his temper at a graduate and gives them a telling-off.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is British and Australian slang for a long harangue.
annotation.definitionFit: Regional slang: a relentless lecture that batters the listener's ears.

entries.clue: Common, and more penniless? Hit wealthy area (11,4)

blocks.note: a stock phrase is a common one

annotation.surface: A commoner even poorer than before lashes out at a rich neighbourhood.
annotation.walkthrough: This is the band of wealthy commuter towns around London. 'Broker' is read as broke plus -er.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British name for affluent suburbs where City financiers live.

entries.clue: Polar station supports work two ways (8)

indicatorNotes.two ways: written two ways means forwards and then backwards
indicatorNotes.supports: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so the station comes last

blocks.note: the same word the other way
a site is a station or position

annotation.surface: A research base at the Pole propping up work in both directions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Polar station' looks like an Antarctic base; 'Polar' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: poles apart, as in polar views.

entries.clue: Response in a trice, surprisingly working (8)

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: the letters come out in a surprising order

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

annotation.surface: A reply that arrived instantly and, unexpectedly, did the job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Working' is not part of the rearranged phrase in the surface, but its letters join the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a reply to something that has happened.

entries.clue: Man spared blundering joiner? (9)

indicatorNotes.blundering: a blundering person stumbles about, and so do the letters

annotation.surface: A clumsy carpenter let off the hook.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Joiner' suggests a carpenter; the question mark admits it is the & sign, which joins words.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: the & sign joins words, so it is a joiner of a kind.

entries.clue: Sprinted – like Blankers-Koen or Joyner-Kersee? (6)

annotation.surface: Two Olympic champions running fast.
annotation.walkthrough: Fanny Blankers-Koen and Jackie Joyner-Kersee were Olympic champion athletes, which makes sprinting feel like the whole story; the second sense is their hyphenated names.
annotation.definitionFit: One sense is running fast; the other describes a name broken by a hyphen.

entries.clue: Crime somewhat irregular, so negligible (5)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: somewhat means to some extent, so only some of the words' letters are used

annotation.surface: An offence so minor and occasional that it hardly counts.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface calls the crime negligible, the last thing anyone would say of setting fires.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: deliberate fire-raising is a crime.

entries.clue: Puck, priest in disguise (6)

indicatorNotes.in disguise: the letters are disguised by rearrangement

annotation.surface: The mischievous Puck dressed up as a clergyman.
annotation.walkthrough: Puck is the mischievous spirit in A Midsummer Night's Dream; a hockey puck is the false lead.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Shakespeare's Puck is a mischievous fairy spirit.

entries.clue: Sweet stream originally running through dry area … (7)

indicatorNotes.originally: originally means at the start, so take the first letter
indicatorNotes.running through: a stream running through land sits inside it

annotation.surface: A pleasant stream flowing across parched land.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 25 across, whose answer describes this dry area.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: in Britain the pudding course is called the sweet.

entries.clue: Bag, container did you say? (4)

indicatorNotes.did you say: asks us to hear the word rather than read it

blocks.note: a vase-like vessel; in a British accent the two words rhyme exactly

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether a bag counts as a container.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bag' looks like a noun beside 'container'; it is the verb, as in bag a prize.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to bag a reward is to get it by effort.

entries.clue: … like this, I see, flowed beyond capital of Sudan (7)

indicatorNotes.beyond: beyond means further along, so the other pieces follow the capital letter

annotation.surface: The Nile flows on past the Sudanese capital, prompting a moment of realisation.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 23 across: 'this' is its dry area, the desert, so the definition means 'like the desert'.
annotation.definitionFit: A cross-reference: 'this' points at 23 across's dry area, and the great African desert is the model.

entries.clue: Not a sausage a European cut up (4)

indicatorNotes.cut: something cut is shortened, so the word loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a Dane with its E cut off

annotation.surface: A European butcher slicing up meat and finding no sausage at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not a sausage' is British slang for nothing at all, so the sausage is not food here.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: Spanish for nothing, matching the British idiom.

entries.clue: Cut in rope and net is damaged (9)

indicatorNotes.is damaged: damaged goods are broken, and so the letters are broken up

annotation.surface: A slash in a rope, and the net is damaged too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut in rope' reads as a noun phrase about a frayed line; 'Cut in' is the verb for interrupting.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to interrupt by putting oneself between others.

entries.clue: Famous, taken down! (5)

annotation.surface: A celebrity humbled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taken down' suggests being humbled; it means written down.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: well known, and recorded in writing.
